Double-blind randomized trial in hospitalized COVID-19 patients found pomegranate tea did not significantly improve hospitalization duration, time to improvement, mortality, respiratory-support duration or symptom severity versus placebo.

Systematic review/meta-analysis of nine RCTs found garlic-based mouthrinses had antimicrobial activity against cariogenic organisms, but effects versus chlorhexidine varied by follow-up and heterogeneity was high; certainty was rated low.

Controlled SHIME gut-model study found a commercial pomegranate extract altered selected microbial taxa and lactate/metabolite patterns in a dose-dependent manner; ex-vivo fermentation evidence should not be presented as a human clinical outcome.

Meta-analysis of 10 randomized trials found celery preparations reduced blood pressure, fasting glucose and triglycerides while total cholesterol, LDL and HDL were not consistently improved; heterogeneous preparations and subgroup dose signals require caution.

Systematic review/meta-analysis found creatine caused a small rise in serum creatinine but no significant deterioration in GFR, supporting the distinction between creatinine turnover and renal impairment; study durations/populations still limit very-long-term certainty.

Systematic review of 98 pediatric neuropsychiatric nutraceutical/phytoceutical trials found adverse-event monitoring and attribution were inconsistently specified, with GI symptoms and headache most commonly reported; safety-reporting quality itself is a major evidence limitation.

Systematic review/case series found serious adverse outcomes among users of Artri King, including Cushing syndrome, adrenal insufficiency and worsened hyperglycemia, consistent with FDA warnings about undeclared diclofenac/dexamethasone; product-safety signal only.

Systematic review summarizes probiotics, omega-3s, CoQ10, vitamin D and polyphenols in rheumatoid arthritis, but heterogeneous interventions, microbiome endpoints and clinical outcomes prevent class-wide treatment conclusions.

Network meta-analysis of 35 RCTs in 838 volleyball athletes ranked β-alanine, creatine and caffeine for selected explosive-performance outcomes, but evidence certainty was low-to-moderate and network rankings should not be treated as universal superiority.

Meta-analysis of 12 studies found some intermittent/daily multiple-micronutrient regimens reduced anemia or iron-deficiency prevalence but did not consistently increase hemoglobin; certainty ranged from very low to moderate and formulations varied.

Large systematic review/meta-analysis of 104 RCTs found standardized turmeric/curcumin supplements improved several glycemic, lipid and inflammatory markers across metabolic conditions, but formulations were highly heterogeneous and often bioavailability-enhanced rather than culinary turmeric.

Network meta-analysis of 19 RCTs compared diverse dietary supplements for androgenetic alopecia; small studies, heterogeneous products and limited direct comparisons constrain rankings and safety/efficacy certainty.

Systematic review/meta-analysis of seven studies found higher vitamin-D regimens raised serum vitamin D and modestly improved HbA1c versus lower doses, while total cholesterol was not significantly different; mixed designs and dose-comparison framing do not justify consumer dosing guidance.

Systematic review of seven RCTs in older adults found curcumin improved selected inflammatory, glycemic, blood-pressure and lipid markers, while other cardiovascular outcomes were inconsistent; formulation/protocol heterogeneity limits broad recommendations.

Review of medicine-food homology bioactives in Parkinson's disease found evidence predominantly preclinical with sparse disease-specific randomized trials and pharmacokinetic limitations for compounds such as curcumin and EGCG; useful translational boundary evidence.

Systematic review of 49 RCTs across rheumatoid, axial spondyloarthritis and psoriatic arthritis found selected diet/supplement signals but substantial heterogeneity prevented meta-analysis; disease-, nutrient- and intervention-specific conclusions must remain separate.

Safety-focused review highlights potential bleeding and drug-interaction concerns with omega-3s, garlic, nattokinase, ginkgo, ginger, ginseng, curcumin and other nutraceuticals, especially with antithrombotic therapy; interaction context should accompany efficacy claims.

Systematic review found 35 of 36 BPC-157 studies were preclinical and only one clinical study was identified; despite growing use, human efficacy/safety remain poorly characterized and professional-sport use is prohibited.

Review summarizes plant sterols, viscous fibers, soy protein, red-yeast rice, berberine, garlic and other cholesterol-lowering food/nutraceutical approaches, but its proposed composite index is conceptual and should not be treated as a validated clinical ranking.

Case-control/cross-sectional analysis found lower serum vitamin E in MS and associations with cognition/disability, but authors explicitly call for longitudinal studies and RCTs before supplementation benefit can be inferred.
Centennial review confirms vitamin E essentiality in deficiency while highlighting persistent uncertainty around broader disease-prevention/therapeutic effects of tocopherols and metabolites.

Large Japanese electronic-record analysis evaluated vitamin E exposure in relation to vancomycin-associated nephrotoxicity; retrospective pharmacoepidemiology should remain association evidence rather than a prophylaxis recommendation.
Two-sample Mendelian-randomization study examined genetically proxied vitamin-E status and depression; genetic causal-inference evidence remains distinct from clinical supplementation trials.

Genetic series identified TTPA-related ataxia with profound vitamin-E deficiency; three of four patients improved after high-dose replacement, supporting disease-specific deficiency treatment rather than general neuroenhancement.

Uncontrolled 60-day selenium-plus-vitamin-E study in ESRD found improved oxidative/inflammatory markers but nonsignificant erythrocyte outcomes; combination and absence of control prevent causal attribution.

Large Chinese cross-sectional study found sex-specific nonlinear associations between plasma vitamin E and homocysteine; U-shaped patterns in men argue against simplistic more-is-better interpretation.

Narrative review of four experimental studies suggests topical vitamin-E-containing formulations may modify acquired enamel pellicle and reduce erosion; evidence is local/topical and largely experimental.
Review describes liposomal/nanoemulsion approaches to improve topical vitamin-E stability and skin penetration; formulation technology evidence does not establish clinical superiority.
Cell-model nanomaterial study combining oxygen delivery, citric acid and vitamin E showed divergent redox effects in healthy versus cancer cells; entirely preclinical and formulation-specific.
Meta-analysis of 49 studies found neither oral nor IV N-acetylcysteine reduced contrast-associated AKI, dialysis or mortality; strong direct null against routine prophylactic benefit.

Randomized trial evaluated NAC for cognitive symptoms during exercise-based cardiac rehabilitation in patients with mild cognitive impairment; co-rehabilitation context requires endpoint-specific interpretation rather than NAC-only generalization.
Genetic/animal/cell study identified SPATA22-related ovarian dysfunction and found NAC partially rescued mouse/cell phenotypes; translational rescue is preclinical, not human fertility efficacy.

Double-blind pilot RCT in youth with NF1 found NAC was generally tolerated but did not improve primary motor, secondary cognitive/behavioral or exploratory biomarker outcomes; two participants stopped for worsening behavior.

Dermatology review describes plausible and early clinical uses of NAC but notes most studies remain small and methodologically limited; condition-specific evidence should not be flattened into broad skin-benefit claims.

Secondary analysis of a 302-person cannabis-use-disorder NAC trial identified heterogeneous craving trajectories associated with psychiatric symptoms and outcomes; craving-class analysis does not demonstrate NAC efficacy.

Double-blind RCT in 50 adolescents found cyclical oral NAC reduced menstrual pain, rescue ibuprofen use and urinary oxidative-stress marker versus placebo; small short study needs independent replication.
Protocol describes a planned double-blind trial of oral NAC for early-onset preeclampsia progression; no efficacy data are available yet.
Human ovarian-tissue xenograft study found oral NAC in mice produced little to no reduction in oxidative stress or follicle-survival improvement; preclinical direct null.
NAC-functionalized dendrimer study improved experimental drug-carrier characteristics and glioma-cell uptake; nanocarrier engineering evidence is unrelated to oral NAC clinical effects.

NAC-enabled inhaled mRNA lipid nanoparticles improved delivery and antitumor immunity in mouse models through surface remodeling/mucolysis; this is platform-preclinical evidence, not systemic NAC anticancer efficacy.
Human-leukocyte in-vitro study found NAC reduced metabolite/ammonia-induced DNA damage in most conditions; cellular protection does not establish clinical benefit in urea-cycle disorders.
Rat/cell hepatocellular-carcinoma study found NAC altered Nrf2/redox and transcriptomic pathways and reduced experimental tumor progression; entirely preclinical.
Targeted fucoidan/NAC nanoparticles improved delayed acetaminophen liver injury in mice by combining antioxidant delivery with neutrophil-recruitment blockade; nanoformulation animal evidence only.
In-vitro endodontic study found NAC medicament altered sealer penetration relative to calcium hydroxide; local dental material interaction is not evidence for systemic NAC effects.

Randomized 8-week study in 30 trained male swimmers found upper-body plyometric training improved performance in both training groups, while beta-alanine produced greater gains in selected power/endurance measures and altered testosterone, cortisol and IgA; co-training design prevents pure supplement attribution.

Placebo-controlled trial in 299 adults found 12 weeks of carnosine produced only selective age/sex-specific endurance signals and no consistent grip-strength benefit; overall effects were limited rather than broadly ergogenic.

Mechanistic review proposes beta-alanine/carnosine buffering and glutamine metabolism as interacting components of muscle-brain crosstalk, but the neuroprotection framework is largely mechanistic and requires direct human validation.

Narrative review identifies beta-alanine, caffeine and carbohydrate mouth rinse as better-supported ergogenic strategies while characterizing BCAA, citrulline, taurine and probiotics as less directly established for perceived-effort-mediated endurance effects.

Narrative review maps protein, caffeine, creatine, beta-alanine, nitrates and peptide-related supplements in older/Masters athletes; useful evidence mapping but not a substitute for intervention-specific systematic review.

Crossover trial in 12 untreated hypertensive men found six days of L-citrulline improved autonomic recovery and reduced resting/post-exercise blood pressure responses after high-intensity exercise; very small male-only study needs replication.

Review describes possible L-citrulline effects on exercise performance, protein synthesis and muscle metabolism but identifies major gaps around strategy, transport, mitochondria and gut-muscle mechanisms.

Perinatal review describes strong metabolic/NO rationale for L-citrulline but emphasizes that adequately powered clinical trials are still needed before routine maternal or neonatal use can be recommended.

Pediatric vascular review summarizes L-citrulline as an investigational nitric-oxide-supporting therapy in systemic/pulmonary vascular disease; disease-specific pharmacotherapy evidence should not be generalized to wellness supplementation.

Review suggests exercise plus L-citrulline may support vascular and muscle outcomes in postmenopausal/older women, but explicitly calls for larger high-quality RCTs and long-term clinical confirmation.

Phase-I study in 10 adults with MELAS found no dose-limiting toxicity across tested L-citrulline doses and exploratory cerebral-blood-flow increases, while high doses raised guanidino compounds; efficacy requires a placebo-controlled trial.

Multicenter 2x2 factorial RCT in 266 ICU adults found resistance training improved function and longer-term outcomes, whereas HMB only modestly improved phase angle and fatigue with no benefit on most outcomes and no synergy with training.

Systematic review/meta-analysis evaluates HMB added to resistance training in older adults across muscle quality, body composition and physical function; retain as category-level synthesis pending source-specific effect extraction.

Randomized crossover trial in 30 active older adults found creatine plus HMB during supervised multicomponent training improved mobility and selected metabolic outcomes versus placebo; combined supplements and exercise prevent component-specific attribution.

Pilot RCT in 21 adults with decompensated cirrhosis found HMB-containing oral nutrition did not significantly improve muscle mass or grip strength versus control, despite within-group improvements in phase angle, arm circumference and chair-stand time.

Thirty-day RCT in older adults with sarcopenia found HMB improved selected muscle measures and adding fructooligosaccharides produced larger intestinal-barrier/inflammatory changes; combination design and short duration limit inference.

Acute human muscle-biopsy study found HMB altered hundreds of transcripts related to protein turnover, amino-acid transport and signaling; transcriptomic response is mechanistic evidence, not proof of long-term functional benefit.

Double-blind crossover study in 24 hemodialysis patients found an HMB+BCAA+zinc medical food improved muscle-thickness/body-composition and selected inflammatory markers but not short-term physical performance; multi-ingredient evidence.

Secondary analysis of a 30-person crossover trial found nominal creatine+HMB effects on glutathione-centered redox measures that did not survive false-discovery correction; exploratory correlations should not be presented as established antioxidant benefit.

Double-blind RCT in 102 adults with obesity found a protein/CaHMB supplement preserved skeletal muscle and improved fat-loss measures during energy restriction versus maltodextrin, but protein co-formulation prevents isolation of HMB-specific effects.

Small nonrandomized study in older adults with obesity, T2D and MASLD found heterogeneous muscle-mass changes during HMB-containing nutrition and no statistically significant overall gain; authors characterize the result as negative and exploratory.

Double-blind crossover study in 17 low-caffeine-consuming men found 300 mg morning caffeine lowered perceived exertion but did not clearly improve repeated sprint, strength, jump, mood or physiologic outcomes under standardized chronobiological conditions.

Sleep-manipulation plus double-blind caffeine study in 41 adolescents found no clear practically meaningful average change in value-based risk decisions from caffeine, sleep restriction or their interaction.

Meta-analysis found caffeine was self-reported as a migraine trigger by about 12% of participants, but heterogeneity exceeded 95% and observational self-report cannot justify universal caffeine avoidance.

Meta-analysis of randomized studies found acute caffeine, especially above 100 mg, transiently increased intraocular pressure in healthy and glaucomatous populations; clinically relevant safety context for susceptible users.

Randomized double-blind crossover trial in 12 adults found a single pre-exercise caffeine dose modestly improved repeated-sprint power for up to 3.5 hours while increasing noradrenaline/heart rate and reducing perceived exertion and muscle pain.

Randomized field crossover trial in 14 trained runners found caffeine increased fat oxidation and reduced perceived exertion during one hour of outdoor running at Fatmax without changing total energy expenditure.

Network meta-analysis of 57 studies found caffeine and carbohydrate mouth rinses improved selected endurance outcomes versus placebo, but caffeine, carbohydrate and menthol did not significantly differ from one another and rankings were outcome-specific.

Double-blind crossover experiments found caffeine increased eccentric loading and subsequent torque reduction when exercise load could rise, but not when load was fixed, suggesting ergogenic output can indirectly increase post-exercise muscle-function loss.

Meta-analysis of 25 studies found caffeine gum produced statistically significant but trivial average performance improvements with low-to-very-low certainty and subgroup-dependent effects; practical significance remains modest.

Randomized crossover trial in 30 male basketball players found 3 mg/kg caffeine did not clearly improve countermovement-jump response after individualized drop-jump conditioning; an isolated subgroup/timepoint signal was exploratory.

Systematic review of 48 human EEG studies found no single reproducible electrophysiological signature of caffeine; alpha/slow-frequency changes were state- and method-dependent and should not be interpreted as direct cognitive improvement.

Randomized crossover study in 13 sedentary women using oral contraceptives found caffeinated coffee increased changes in fat oxidation during/after exercise versus decaf, but the sample was very small and focused on substrate use rather than performance.

Meta-analysis of seven randomized military studies found acute caffeine improved vigilance, response speed, complex cognition and task performance during sleep loss, with the most consistent effects on vigilance/response outcomes.

Double-blind crossover trial in 16 resistance-trained women found caffeine increased knee-extensor peak torque, with exploratory evidence that menstrual phase modified some strength effects; most other neuromuscular outcomes showed no phase interaction.

Three-level meta-analysis of seven CrossFit studies found a small favorable effect of acute caffeine on performance and higher lactate, with no clear moderation by training status or delivery protocol; evidence remains limited and male-dominant.

Four-arm crossover trial found caffeine improved repeated-sprint running and reduced perceived exertion while acute blackcurrant powder did not, and combining them produced no additive performance benefit.

Scoping review of ten RCTs suggests neuromuscular electrical stimulation plus protein may improve muscle mass/strength in older or mobility-limited adults, but most studies were only fair quality and combined-intervention effects cannot isolate protein.

Narrative review supports whey-plus-exercise for muscle/physical outcomes in older adults but finds cognitive and injury-prevention evidence limited and inconsistent, with many outcomes secondary rather than prespecified.

Retrospective study associated whey plus a Mediterranean-style diet with better muscle and selected cognitive outcomes in sarcopenic older adults, but nonrandomized diet co-intervention prevents causal whey-specific inference.

Nine-person randomized crossover trial found almond- and whey-protein beverages produced comparable acute appetite, GI and hydration responses in postmenopausal women; tiny sample and acute endpoints limit broader conclusions.

Randomized metabolic study in 45 older men found 20 g of soy-pea protein, leucine-fortified plant protein, or whey did not increase muscle-protein-synthesis rates versus postabsorptive values; protein quality differences did not rescue the low-dose anabolic response.

Scoping review of 14 adult studies found protein supplements produced inconsistent, mostly modest microbiome/metabolite changes and no consistent gut-barrier or inflammatory effect; co-interventions were common and isolated protein effects remain unclear.

Six-month double-blind RCT in 74 healthy adults with exercise-related joint discomfort found undenatured type-II collagen improved selected KOOS domains earlier than placebo and altered recovery time/CTX-II in subgroups; subgroup dependence warrants caution.

Randomized placebo-controlled trial in 114 women found a specific low-molecular-weight fish collagen peptide improved cellulite, skin elasticity/roughness and hair diameter over 24 weeks; effects are formulation-specific and cosmetic rather than general collagen equivalence.

Pilot double-blind RCT in 22 adults found gelatin did not produce significant group-by-time improvements in soreness, torque or collagen-turnover markers after eccentric exercise; selected pairwise signals were exploratory.

Narrative review finds oral collagen has the most consistent signals for skin hydration/elasticity and wrinkle appearance but highlights short duration, heterogeneous products, multi-ingredient formulas and industry funding as major confidence limits.

Systematic review of 19 studies found carbohydrate-electrolyte beverages generally rehydrated exercise-associated dehydration better than water, with substantial protocol variability and no single universal formulation established.

Randomized crossover study in 12 participants found a sweat-loss-personalized hydration strategy improved fluid replacement and prolonged high-intensity exercise in heat versus ad-lib commercial electrolyte drink; the strategy changed both fluid volume and sodium replacement.

Randomized 21-km running study in 14 trained men found a BCAA-containing electrolyte beverage improved hydration/potassium balance and post-run soreness/strength versus some comparators but did not improve final-5-km completion time; multi-ingredient beverage evidence.

Case report of large 7-hydroxymitragynine ingestion described profound CNS depression, marked QTc prolongation and prolonged encephalopathy requiring intensive care; polysubstance and psychiatric/infectious contributors make causality multifactorial but the toxicity signal is serious.

Focused clinical review emphasizes that expanding US kratom use is occurring amid unregulated product variability, limited high-quality safety/efficacy data and increasing need for clinician recognition of use, dependence and toxicity.

Human cross-sectional metabolomics study of 37 regular kratom users versus 12 controls found distinct plasma metabolite/pathway profiles involving amino-acid, pyruvate, TCA, glycolytic and glutathione metabolism; association does not establish harm or benefit.

Meta-analysis of 21 studies estimated low general-population but substantially higher high-risk/substance-using kratom prevalence, with major regional and methodological heterogeneity; surveillance evidence, not efficacy or toxicity.

Review distinguishes native leaf from increasingly concentrated extracts, isolates and 7-OH-enriched or chemically altered products and argues dependence/overdose risk likely rises as alkaloid concentration and product modification increase.

Perinatal review/case discussion describes maternal and neonatal withdrawal risk and very limited evidence for buprenorphine management of kratom use disorder in pregnancy; only a few pregnancy cases support current practice.

Validated human plasma assay quantified 12 kratom alkaloids and five mitragynine metabolites, showing rapid absorption and identifying major circulating alkaloids/metabolites in regular users; high-value source-identity and PK evidence.

Cross-sectional treatment sample of 403 men found kratom-use indicators were not overall risk factors for methamphetamine craving; only a subgroup association with age at first kratom use emerged in those with heroin history.

Narrative toxicology review describes opioid-like toxidromes, variable naloxone responsiveness, possible delayed/recurrent respiratory depression, polysubstance amplification and substantial product heterogeneity; clinical management evidence remains case-heavy.

Cardiovascular review integrates ion-channel mechanisms with reported tachycardia, hypertension, QTc prolongation, Brugada patterns, ventricular arrhythmias and cardiac arrest while emphasizing heterogeneous products and confounding co-exposures.

American College of Medical Toxicology position statement identifies public-health risks from 7-hydroxymitragynine and other kratom-associated compounds; authoritative toxicology guidance rather than an efficacy study.

Self-selected US survey of 136 kratom consumers found cancer and non-cancer users differed in motivations and patterns, with cancer respondents frequently using kratom for pain/mental-health concerns; perceptions cannot establish effectiveness or safety.

Systematic review of 24 clinical/forensic reports classified kratom-associated diffuse alveolar hemorrhage, ARDS/lung injury, eosinophilic pneumonitis, respiratory depression and postmortem pulmonary edema; evidence remains case/forensic based but clinically important.
Case report describes transient sensorineural hearing loss, rhabdomyolysis, severe AKI and dialysis in a chronic kratom user; sepsis and other clinical factors limit single-agent causal certainty.

Case report describes seizure-like activity and refractory pulseless ventricular tachycardia after concentrated kratom extract, requiring prolonged resuscitation and VA-ECMO; toxicology confirmed mitragynine.

Six-day randomized double-blind placebo-controlled trial of a commercial kava/kratom liquid blend found mostly mild-to-moderate adverse events and no major laboratory toxicity in healthy adults; short duration and combined-product design cannot establish long-term safety.

Case report links very heavy kava tea ingestion with biopsy-proven severe acute tubulointerstitial nephritis, marked creatinine rise, bradycardia and QT prolongation, with recovery after corticosteroids; product analysis found kavalactones without other detected substances.
Published report documents acute kava-associated skin toxicity; preserve as a rare safety signal while avoiding incidence estimates from case-level evidence.

Pediatric case report describes prolonged serotonin-syndrome features during kava use while switching serotonergic antidepressants, with plausible CYP2D6/MAO interaction mechanisms; single-case evidence supports interaction caution, not frequency estimates.

Case report describes hallucinations, anxiety, insomnia and myoclonus after stopping heavy kava/kratom beverage use, with GABAergic withdrawal suspected and improvement after phenobarbital/diazepam; mixed-product exposure complicates attribution.

Narrative systematic review of 197 records found kava's cultural/economic importance clear but health benefits and harms—including anxiety and liver effects—remain inconsistent and methodologically limited.
Three-patient case series found acute kava reactions resembling DRESS with distinctive sebaceous adenitis/apoptosis on biopsy; rare dermatologic safety signal without incidence data.

Large US survey estimated 10.7% past-year kava use among respondents and common co-use with prescription/alternative products; perceived relaxation benefits and drowsiness/sweating are self-report observational findings.

Online survey of adults using kava/kratom found past-year SUD criteria much more common for kratom than kava and substantial co-use; self-selected sampling and DSM-criterion adaptation require cautious interpretation.

US poison-center analysis tracked rising tianeptine exposures from 2015–2023 and associated clinical outcomes, providing national toxicovigilance evidence for misuse and toxicity rather than controlled incidence estimates.

New Jersey poison-center outbreak identified 34 patients with severe toxicity after tianeptine products; product testing found variable composition including synthetic cannabinoids, kava alkaloids and cannabinoids, and many patients required intubation/ICU care.

Online survey found tianeptine use uncommon within a gray-market-product sample but frequently associated with rapid tolerance, adverse effects, severe past-year SUD criteria and strong perceived addictiveness/overdose risk; self-selected sample limits prevalence inference.

Case report describes concomitant tianeptine and alcohol use disorders treated with buprenorphine-naloxone; single-patient management evidence supports clinical awareness without establishing an optimal protocol.

Case report and review describes severe tianeptine use disorder with psychiatric deterioration, dependence and withdrawal, emphasizing diagnostic barriers and need for addiction-treatment referral; case-level evidence only.

Systematic review of 25 studies found frequent habitual misuse, overdose, withdrawal and co-use, with naloxone and buprenorphine appearing in reported management; underlying literature is largely case-based and heterogeneous.

Three-case series and review describes rapid tolerance, opioid-like intoxication/withdrawal and use of naloxone, buprenorphine, clonidine and supportive care; treatment conclusions remain limited by case evidence.

Systematic review of 53 publications found opioid-like dependence, withdrawal and overdose, with substantial ICU use in retrospective series and reported fatalities among detailed overdose cases; evidence is dominated by case reports/series.

Case report describes severe hypoxemic respiratory failure, encephalopathy and pulmonary infiltrates after combined kratom/tianeptine ingestion, improving with naloxone and ICU supportive care; co-exposure prevents single-agent attribution.

NLP-assisted qualitative analysis of Reddit posts found increasing discussion of tianeptine dependence, withdrawal and co-ingestion; useful real-world signal but self-reported social-media content cannot estimate clinical incidence.

Survey of addiction-conference clinicians found substantial knowledge gaps around kratom, phenibut and tianeptine despite high concern and support for more research/regulation; clinician-practice context rather than toxicity incidence.

Case report describes sustained abstinence from tianeptine after methadone treatment when high-dose buprenorphine had not controlled cravings/withdrawal; illustrates a treatment gap but cannot establish comparative efficacy.

Laboratory analysis found none of 12 US sports supplements labeled with Eria jarensis were accurately labeled; several contained undeclared stimulants, including FDA-prohibited DMAA, and caffeine content varied dramatically.

Review summarizes laboratory risk-mitigation approaches for dietary-supplement adulteration, including identity/purity testing, supplier quality agreements and third-party verification; quality-system evidence rather than clinical efficacy.

Review of authentication methods for botanicals in plant extracts and supplements highlights identity testing as a core defense against substitution and adulteration; methodological quality-control evidence.
Review documents the problem of sports supplements adulterated with anabolic steroids and the anti-doping/health consequences of undeclared exposure; product-quality and harm-reduction evidence.

US market analysis found wide deviations in Rhodiola rosavin/salidroside content, probable undisclosed synthetic salidroside in one product and trace metals in tested products; strong formulation/authenticity warning.
Analytical study applies LC-MS/MS and LC-QTOF/MS screening for anabolic-androgenic steroids in illicit dietary supplements/counterfeit drugs; useful adulterant-detection and quality-control evidence.
Post-market analysis of 65 online Cordyceps products found more than half falsified, 11% unregistered and 6.2% adulterated with corticosteroids, alongside frequent illegal disease claims.
Validated GC-MS method targets undeclared diuretics in adulterated weight-loss supplements, supporting forensic/product-quality surveillance rather than efficacy claims.
Analysis of 23 green-coffee-bean supplements found wide chlorogenic-acid/caffeine variability, products labeled 50% CGAs with none detected, and decaffeinated products exceeding caffeine thresholds.

Analytical chemistry study isolated previously unreported tadalafil analogues illegally added to a male sexual herbal supplement, demonstrating pharmaceutical adulteration of purportedly herbal products.
Toxicovigilance report documents multiple batches of a slimming supplement adulterated with sibutramine and associated clinical cases; high-value undeclared-drug safety signal.

Case report describes yellow-oleander toxicity from a misrepresented dietary supplement, underscoring that botanical/product identity failures can cause severe poisoning independent of labeled intent.

Case report attributes drug-induced liver injury to a turmeric supplement containing piperine after competing causes were evaluated; single-case evidence supports hepatotoxicity vigilance, especially with bioavailability-enhancing formulations.

Safety review focuses on reproductive, thyroid and immune-system concerns relevant to ashwagandha use as a food/additive, emphasizing unresolved risk questions and the need for population-specific caution.
